Surah "Az-Zumar" (The Throngs)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The revelation of the Book﴾: i.e., the Qur'an. It is a mubtada' (grammatical subject), and its khabar (predicate) is:

﴿from Allah﴾: i.e., it was sent down from Allah's presence. Or it is the khabar of an omitted mubtada'. The prepositional phrase "مِنَ اللهِ" (min Allah) is either a ṣila (complement) of the verbal noun تَنْزِيلُ (tanzil, "revelation"), or not a complement, but rather a khabar following another khabar, or the khabar of an omitted mubtada'. Its estimated form is: "This is the revelation of the Book, this is from Allah."

﴿the All-Mighty﴾: in His dominion.

﴿the All-Wise﴾: in His management.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 2:

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾. This is not a repetition, because the first (statement) serves as a title for the Book, and the second (statement) serves to explain what is in the Book.

﴿So worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾: (mukhlisan) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, indicating the state of the subject during the action).

﴿To Him is the religion﴾, meaning: making the religion pure for Him from shirk (association of partners with Allah) and riyā' (showing off), through tawḥīd (affirmation of Allah's oneness) and purifying the inner intention. Here al-dīn (the religion) is in the accusative case, governed by (mukhlisan).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 3:

﴿Surely, to Allah belongs the pure religion.﴾ That is: He is the One who is due to be singled out, so that obedience is purified for Him from every trace of impurity, because He has knowledge of the unseen and the secrets. From Qatadah: "The pure religion is the testimony that there is no god but Allah." From al-Hasan: "It is Islam."

﴿And those who take protectors besides Him⁠—﴾ That is: gods. This is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is omitted. Its estimated form is: "And those who worshipped idols say: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness.﴾" (zulfa is a verbal noun, meaning: bringing near.)

﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them⁠—﴾ between the Muslims and the polytheists

﴿concerning that over which they differ.﴾ It was said: when the Muslims would say to them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would say, "Allah." Then when they said to them, "Why then do you worship idols?!" they would say, "We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness." The meaning is that Allah will judge on the Day of Resurrection between the disputing parties from both groups.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and a disbeliever.﴾ That is: He does not guide one whom He knows will choose disbelief. That is to say, He does not grant him success in guidance, nor does He help him at the time of his choosing disbelief; rather He forsakes him. Their lying is their saying, concerning some of those whom they took as protectors besides Allah, that they are "the daughters of Allah." Therefore He followed it, arguing against them, with His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 4:

﴿If Allah had wished to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He willed.﴾ That is: if it were permissible to take a son in the way you suppose, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He willed, not what you choose and will.

﴿Glory be to Him﴾: He declared His essence far above having any of what they ascribed to Him of associates (awliya'), and of sons (awlad). He indicated this by His saying: ﴿He is Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ (al-Qahhar). That is, He is One, free from being joined to numbers, exalted above division and begetting, the Subduer who overpowers everything; and among things are their gods. So how could He have associates (awliya') and partners?! Then He indicated, through the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the wrapping of each of the two alternations (al-malawayn, the night and the day) over the other, and the subjection of the two luminaries (al-nayyirayn, the sun and the moon) and their running for a specified term, and the dispersal of people, numerous as they are, from a single soul, and the creation of the cattle, that He is One, not shared, the Subduer, not overcome, by His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 5:

﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth. He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night.﴾ Al-takwir (the wrapping, folding over) means al-laff (wrapping around) and al-layy (twisting around). It is said: "He wound the turban (al-'imamah) on his head and wrapped it (kawwarahā)."

(p-170) The meaning is that each of them (night and day) conceals the other when it comes upon it. So its concealing of the other is likened to an apparent thing wrapped around something, which hides what it covers from the sight of eyes. And [the meaning is also] that this one returns upon that one in a continuous returning, so that is likened to the successive coils of a turban, one upon the trace of another.

﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a term specified.﴾

That is: the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Unquestionably, He is the Mighty (al-'Aziz)﴾, the Overpowering, the Able to punish whoever does not take heed from the subjugation of the sun and the moon, and so does not believe in the One who subjected them.

﴿the Forgiving (al-Ghaffar)﴾, to whoever reflects and takes heed, and so believes in the One who arranges them both.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 39 (*al-Zumar*), verse 6:

﴿He created you from a single soul﴾, i.e., Adam, peace be upon him,

﴿then made from it its mate﴾, i.e., Hawwa' (Eve), from his *qusayra* (the lowest floating ribs). It is said that He brought forth the offspring of Adam from his back like *dharr* (tiny particles, like specks of dust), and then created Hawwa' after that.

﴿then made from it its mate, and sent down for you of the cattle﴾. I.e., He made, according to al-Hasan, or He created her in the Garden with Adam, peace be upon him, and then sent her down. Or, because she cannot live except on plants, and plants cannot subsist except by water, and He has sent down water, it is as if He sent her down.

﴿eight pairs﴾, male and female, of the camels, the cattle, the sheep, and the goats, as explained in the surah "al-An'am" (chapter 6). A *zawj* (pair, mate) is the name for one thing that has another with it. When it stands alone, it is *fard* (single) and *watr* (odd).

﴿eight pairs. He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation﴾: a drop (*nutfah*), then a clot (*'alaqah*), then a lump of flesh (*mudghah*), then up to the completion of creation.

﴿in three darknesses﴾: the darkness of the belly, the womb, and the *mashima* (the membrane enclosing the fetus). Or: the darkness of the loins (*sulb*), the belly, and the womb.

﴿That is﴾, the One whose these acts are, ﴿Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the kingdom. There is no god but He. So how are you turned away?﴾ That is, how are you diverted from worshipping Him to worshipping other than Him? Then He made clear that He is free of need of them, by His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 7:

﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is Free of need from you﴾, (Free of need) from your faith, while you are in need of Him, because of the harm you suffer through disbelief and the benefit you gain through faith.

﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾, because disbelief is not pleasing to Allah (Exalted is He), even though it occurs by His will.

﴿And if you give thanks﴾, by believing,

﴿He approves it for you﴾, i.e., He approves your thanks for you, because it is the cause of your success, so He will reward you with Paradise for it. "Yarduhu" with a damma on the ha' and with the full vowel (ishba'), is the reading of Makki and Ali. "Yarḍahu" with a damma on the ha' without the full vowel is the reading of Nafi', Hisham, and Asim except Yahya and Hammad. The others read "yarḍahu" with a sukun on the ha'.

﴿And no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾, i.e., no one is held accountable for the sin of another.

﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾, the return of you all is to the recompense of your Lord.

﴿So He will inform you of what you used to do﴾, He will tell you of your deeds and will recompense you for them.

﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾, of the hidden things of the hearts.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 8:

﴿And when harm touches man﴾, [i.e., Abu Jahl, or every disbeliever],

﴿harm﴾, affliction and hardship; and "touching" (al-mass) in regard to conditions is a metaphor (majaz),

﴿he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance﴾, returning to Allah with supplication, calling upon no one other than Him,

﴿then when He bestows upon him﴾, gives him,

﴿a favour from Him﴾, from Allah, Mighty and Majestic,

﴿he forgets what he used to call upon Him for before﴾, i.e., he forgets his Lord whom he used to entreat humbly. And "ma" here carries the meaning of "man" (who), as in His saying: ﴿and by Him who created the male and the female﴾ [al-Layl: 3]. Or it means: he forgets the harm for which he used to call upon Allah to remove it.

﴿And he sets up rivals to Allah﴾, equals (amthal),

﴿so that he may lead astray﴾, read as "liyaḍilla" by Makki, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub,

﴿from His way﴾, i.e., Islam.

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad,

﴿"Enjoy yourself﴾, an imperative of threat,

﴿with your disbelief for a little while﴾, i.e., in this world,

﴿indeed you are among the companions of the Fire﴾, among its people.

"Am man" (or "Is it one who"). Makki, Nafi' and Hamza read it with a light pronunciation (takhfif), placing the interrogative hamza (the question particle) before "man." Others read it with emphasis (tashdid), placing "am" before it. "Man" is the subject (mubtada', the topic of the sentence), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted. Its implied form is: "Am man huwa qanitun ka-ghayrihi?!" meaning: "Is one who is obedient like one who is disobedient?" The qanit is the one who is obedient to God. It is omitted because the context indicates it, namely the mention of the disbeliever before it, and the statement after it: ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ ﴿in the hours of the night﴾, its periods,

﴿prostrating and standing﴾: two circumstantial accusatives (hal, a word describing the state of the subject) referring to the pronoun in "qanit,"

﴿fearing the Hereafter﴾, meaning the punishment of the Hereafter,

﴿and hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾, meaning Paradise. The verse indicates that the believer must be between fear and hope: he hopes for His mercy, not for his own deeds, and fears His punishment because of his shortcomings in his deeds. Then, if hope exceeds its limit, it becomes complacency, and if fear exceeds its limit, it becomes despair. God the Exalted has said: ﴿None feels secure from the plan of God except the losing people﴾ [al-A'raf: 99], and He said: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of God except the disbelieving people﴾ [Yusuf: 87]. Therefore neither of them should exceed its limit.

﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾, meaning: those who know and act upon it. It is as if He made the one who does not act not a person of knowledge. In this there is a great rebuke of those who acquire knowledge and then do not devote themselves (qanit) to it, and who are tested through it, and then are tested by the worldly life. They are, in God's sight, ignorant, since He made the obedient ones the scholars. Or it is intended as a comparison, meaning: just as the knowledgeable and the ignorant are not equal, so the obedient and the disobedient are not equal.

﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾: "ulu al-albab" is the plural of "lubb," meaning: only those of intellect are admonished by God's admonition.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 10:

﴿Say: O My servants who believe﴾, without the yā' (in the vocative), according to most readers,

﴿fear your Lord﴾, by complying with His commands and avoiding His prohibitions,

﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾. That is: those who obey God in the world. The phrase "fī" (in) is connected to "aḥsanū" (did good), not to "ḥasanah" (good). Its meaning: those who did good in this world, for them there is good in the Hereafter, which is entry into Paradise, that is, a good that cannot be described. Al-Suddi connected it to "ḥasanah" and interpreted the good as health and well-being. The meaning of ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾ is that there is absolutely no excuse for those who fall short in doing good, even if they plead that they cannot devote themselves to doing good in their homelands. It is said to them: indeed God's earth is spacious and His lands are many, so migrate to other lands, and follow the example of the prophets and the righteous in their migration to lands other than their own, so that they may increase their good deeds upon their good deeds and their obedience upon their obedience.

﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward﴾, for leaving their homelands and their tribes, and for other things, swallowing bitter ordeals (p-173) and bearing trials in obedience to God and in seeking increased good,

﴿their reward without measure﴾. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him: "The reckoning of the reckoners cannot reach it, nor can it be known." It is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "ajr" (reward), meaning: abundantly provided.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 11:

﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾, that is, to worship Allah,

﴿sincerely devoting the religion to Him﴾. That is: I have been commanded to devote the religion (dīn) sincerely.

﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾. And I have been commanded to this for the purpose that I be the first of the Muslims, i.e., their leader and foremost of them in this world and the Hereafter. The meaning is that sincere devotion (al-ikhlas) to Him has precedence in this world; whoever is sincere is foremost. So the first (command) is an order to worship together with sincere devotion, and the second is an order to be foremost. Because their two aspects differ, they are treated as two different things, and so it is correct to conjoin one of them to the other.

Say: "Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day." (This is said) to those who invited you to return to the religion of your fathers. That is because the disbelievers of Quraysh said to him, peace and blessings be upon him: "Do you not look at your father and your grandfather and the chiefs of your people, who worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza?!" So this was revealed in response to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 14:

﴿Say, "It is Allah I worship, devoted to Him in my religion."﴾ This verse is an informing that He singles out Allah alone for His worship, devoting His religion to Him, to the exclusion of anything else. The first [statement] is an informing that he is commanded to worship and to devotion (ikhlas, sincerity of intention). So the speech first concerns the act itself and its affirmation, and secondly concerns the one for whose sake the act is performed. Accordingly, He followed it with His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 15:

﴿So worship what you will besides Him﴾. This is a command of threat. It was said to him: "If you oppose the religion of your fathers, you will have lost." So there was revealed: ﴿Say: Indeed, the losers﴾, that is, those who are complete in loss, encompassing its aspects and its causes,

﴿who have lost themselves﴾, by destroying them in the Fire,

﴿and their families﴾, that is, and they have lost their families,

﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, because they misled them, so they all went to the Fire. He described their loss with the utmost severity in His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾, where He opened the sentence with the particle of alerting (ألا), placed the separating pronoun (al-fasl) between the subject and the predicate, defined the word "loss" (الخسران), and qualified it with "al-mubin" (the manifest), and that is because they exchanged Paradise for the Fire, and the lofty ranks for the lowest depths.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 16:

﴿For them there will be canopies of fire above them⦆ — that is, layers (aṭbāq).

﴿and beneath them canopies⦆ — that is, layers of fire. And they are canopies for others (below them), meaning: the Fire encompasses them from every side.

﴿That⦆ — the punishment that has been described, or that the canopies (are the means) by which

﴿God frightens His servants⦆ — so that they will believe in it and avoid what He has forbidden.

﴿O My servants, so fear Me⦆ — and do not expose yourselves to what brings about My wrath. He frightened them with the Fire, then warned them of Himself.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 17:

﴿And those who avoid the Taghut⁠—﴾ al-Shayatin (the devils). "Fa'lut" from "al-Tughyan" (transgression), like "al-Malakut" and "al-Rahamut," except that in it there is a metathesis (qalb), with the lam placed before the ayn. It is applied to the Shaytan, or to the Shayatin, because "al-Taghut" is a masdar (verbal noun). In it there are intensive forms (mubalaghat): one is naming by the masdar, as if the very essence of the Shaytan is transgression; and another is that the pattern is that of intensification (bina' mubalaghah), for "al-Rahamut" is the vast mercy, and "al-Malakut" is the extended dominion. The qalb (metathesis) is for specification (li'l-ikhtisas), since it is not applied to anything other than the Shaytan. The intended meaning here is the plural. And it has been read: "al-Tawaghit."

﴿that they should not worship it﴾: a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) from "al-Taghut," meaning: its worship.

﴿and turn back in repentance﴾: returned.

﴿to God; for them is good news﴾: it is the glad tidings of reward, which the angels receive them with at the time of the presence of death, bringing good news, and when they are gathered (on the Day of Resurrection).

﴿So give good news to My servants﴾

﴿Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾: they are the ones who have avoided (*ijtanabu*) and turned penitently (*anabu*) to God. He intended by them that they should be in this attribute together with avoidance and penitence, so the apparent noun (*al-zahir*, the explicit noun) was placed in the position of the pronoun (*al-damir*, the pronoun). He intended that they should be critics (*nuqqad*) in religion, distinguishing between the good (*hasan*) and the better (*ahsan*), and between the virtuous (*fadil*) and the most virtuous (*afdal*). So when two matters confront them, one obligatory (*wajib*, what is required) and one recommended (*nadb*, what is encouraged), they choose the obligatory. Likewise with the permissible (*mubah*) and the recommended, being eager for what is closer to God and greater in reward. Or it means: they listen to the Qur'an and other things, and follow the Qur'an. Or they listen to the commands of God and follow the best of them, such as retaliation (*qisas*) and pardon (*afw*), and the like. Or they listen to speech in a gathering (p-175) of people in which there are good and bad points, so they relate the best of what they heard and refrain from the rest.

﴿Those are the ones whom God has guided, and those are the people of understanding﴾: that is, those who benefit by their intellects.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 19:

﴿Is one against whom the word of punishment has been decreed—will you then save one who is in the Fire?﴾ The original form of the sentence is: "Is one against whom the word of punishment has been decreed—i.e., it has become binding—will you then save him?!" It is a conditional sentence (jumlah shartiyyah), into which the interrogative hamzah of denial (hamzat al-inkar) has entered, and the fa' is the fa' of the response (fa' al-jaza'). Then the fa' that comes at its beginning entered for conjunction (li'l-'atf) upon an elided element, whose estimated form is: "Are you the master of their affair, so that whoever has the word of punishment decreed against him, will you save him?!" The second hamzah is the first one, repeated to emphasize the meaning of denial. The phrase "man fi al-nar" (whoever is in the Fire) has been placed in the position of the pronoun, i.e., "will you save him?" Thus, according to this, the verse is a single sentence. Or its meaning is: "Is one against whom the word of punishment has been decreed going to be saved from it?! Will you then save him?!" That is, no one is able to save the one whom Allah has led astray and whom His knowledge has already determined to be among the people of the Fire.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 20:

﴿But those who have feared their Lord, for them are chambers, above them are chambers built high, beneath which rivers flow﴾. That is: for them are lofty dwellings in Paradise, and above them are dwellings even loftier than these. Meaning: for the disbelievers there are canopies of Fire, and for the God-fearing there are chambers.

﴿Built high, beneath which rivers flow﴾. That is: beneath their dwellings.

﴿The promise of Allah; Allah does not fail in His promise﴾. "The promise of Allah" is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid), because His saying "for them are chambers" carries the meaning of "Allah has promised them that."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 21:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾, meaning rain. It was also said: all water in the earth comes from the sky; it descends from it to the rock, and then Allah distributes it,

﴿and makes it flow﴾, that is, He makes it enter,

﴿as springs in the earth﴾, meaning fountains, channels, and watercourses, like the veins in bodies. "Yanabi'" (springs) is in the accusative, either as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or as an adverbial of place (ẓarf). "Fi al-ard" (in the earth) is a qualifier (ṣifah) of "yanabi'".

﴿Then He brings forth thereby﴾, by the water,

﴿crops of varying colors﴾, meaning their forms: green, red, yellow, and white; or their kinds: wheat, barley, sesame, and other things,

﴿then it withers﴾, it dries up,

﴿so you see it turned yellow﴾, after its freshness and beauty,

﴿then He makes it debris﴾, crumbled and broken pieces. Ḥuṭām is what has crumbled and broken apart of plants and other things,

﴿Indeed in that﴾, in the sending down of water and the bringing forth of crops,

﴿is a reminder for those of understanding﴾, a reminder and an alert that there must be a wise Maker, and that this occurs by measure and management, not by neglect and idleness.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 22:

﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord...?﴾ That is: He expanded his breast ﴿to Islam﴾, and so he was guided. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about expansion (sharh), and he said: "When the light enters the heart, it expands and becomes spacious." It was said: "Is there a sign of that?" He said: "Yes: turning in repentance to the abode of eternity (al-khuld), withdrawing from the abode of delusion (al-ghurur), and preparing for death before death arrives."

﴿So he is upon a light from his Lord﴾: upon clear proof (bayan) and insight (basirah). The meaning is: "Is he whose breast Allah has expanded, so that he is guided, like one whose heart has been sealed and whose heart has hardened?!" The second part has been omitted, because His saying ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened﴾ indicates it.

﴿Against the remembrance of Allah﴾: that is, from abandoning the remembrance of Allah, or on account of the remembrance of Allah; that is, when Allah or His signs are mentioned in their presence, their hearts increase in hardness. This is like His saying: ﴿So it increased them in defilement upon their defilement﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125]. ﴿Those are in manifest error﴾: clear misguidance.

God has sent down the most beautiful statement. The placing of the name of God as the subject (mubtada') or the construction of "nazzala" upon it, indicates the magnification of "the most beautiful statement."

"A Book" is either a substitute (badal) for "the most beautiful statement," or a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it.

"Similar, oft-repeated" (mutashabihan): some of it resembles some other part in truthfulness, clarity, admonition, wisdom, inimitability (i'jaz), and other respects.

"Oft-repeated" (mathani): an adjective (na't) of "a Book," the plural of "mathna," meaning "repeated and reiterated," because it repeats its stories, reports, rulings, commands, prohibitions, promises, threats, and admonitions. It is thus an explanation of its being "similar," since repeated stories and other material can only be similar. It is also said: it is called mathani because it is repeated in recitation, so it is never tiresome. The describing of a single thing with a plural form is permissible because the Book is a whole with details, and the details of a thing are its whole. Do you not see (p-177) that you say: "The Qur'an consists of sevens, fifths, surahs, and verses"? Likewise you say: "Stories, rulings, and admonitions, repeated." Alternatively, it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of "similar," as you say: "I saw a handsome man in features," and the meaning is: "its oft-repeated parts being similar."

"Shiver" (taqsha'irru): tremble and move.

"From it the skins of those who fear their Lord": it is said, "the skin shivered" (iqsha''arra al-jild) when it contracts with intense tightening. The meaning is that when they hear the Qur'an and its verses of threat, a fear comes upon them, and their skins shiver from it. In a hadith: "When the skin of the believer shivers from fear of God, his sins fall away from him as leaves fall from a dry tree."

"Then their skins and hearts soften to the remembrance of God": that is, when verses of mercy are mentioned, their skins and hearts become soft, and what fear and shivering had been upon them departs. It is construed with "ila" because it includes the meaning of a verb that takes "ila," as if it were said: "they became at rest, soft toward the remembrance of God, not constricted." Mention is restricted to the remembrance of God without mention of mercy, because His mercy precedes His wrath; so, because His mercy is primary, when God is mentioned nothing comes to mind but that He is Compassionate and Merciful. The skins are mentioned alone first, then the hearts are joined with them second, because the locus of fear is the heart, so mentioning it includes mention of the hearts.

"That": a reference to the Book, which is "the guidance of God, by which He guides whom He wills" among His servants, namely whom He knows to choose guidance.

"And whoever God leaves astray": He creates misguidance in him.

"For him there is no guide": to the truth.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 24:

﴿Is then he who shields with his face from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [is equal to one who is safe from the punishment?]. The predicate has been omitted, as it is omitted in its counterparts, and it is understood as "like one who is safe from the punishment." "Evil of the punishment" (sū' al-'adhāb) means its severity. The meaning is that when a person encounters something frightening among frightening things, he meets it with his hand and seeks to shield his face with it, because the face is the most precious of his limbs to him. Whoever is thrown into the Fire is thrown with his hands shackled to his neck, so he cannot protect himself from the Fire except with his face, which he had been protecting from other dangers with other parts of his body, as a safeguard for it and a defense for it. (p-178) ﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the guardians of the Fire will say to them:

﴿Taste﴾ the consequence of ﴿what you used to earn﴾, that is, your earning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 25:

﴿Those before them denied, so the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.﴾ "Those before them" refers to those before the Quraysh.

﴿So the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.﴾ From the direction they did not expect, and it did not occur to them that evil would come to them from it, while they were secure, when they were taken by surprise from their place of safety.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 26:

﴿So Allah made them taste disgrace﴾: al-khizy, meaning humiliation and abasement, such as being transformed (al-maskh), being swallowed up by the earth (al-khasf), being killed, being exiled (al-jala'), and similar punishments from Allah.

﴿In the life of this world. But the punishment of the Hereafter is greater﴾: greater than the punishment of this world.

﴿If only they knew﴾: they would have believed.
﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, that they might remember.﴾ (So that) they might take admonition.

Qur'an in Arabic, a emphatic circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl muʼakkida), as you say: "Zayd came to me as a righteous man (rajulan ṣāliḥan), and a sensible human being (insānan ʿāqilan)," where you mention "a man" or "a human being" for emphasis; or it is in the accusative of praise (naṣb ʿalā al-madḥ).

Ghayra dhī ʿiwajin: upright (mustaqīman), free from contradiction (tanāquḍ) and disagreement (ikhtilāf). He did not say "mustaqīman" (upright) for the sake of indicating that there is no crookedness (ʿiwaj) in it at all. It was also said: the meaning of ʿiwaj here is doubt (shakk).

La-ʿallahum yattaqūn: [so that] they may fear (yattaqūn) disbelief (al-kufr).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 29:

﴿God strikes a parable: a man﴾, a substitution (badal),

﴿in whom are partners disputing with one another (mutashakisun)﴾, meaning: quarrelling, disagreeing,

﴿and a man wholly (salaman) belonging﴾, a verbal noun (masdar) of "silm", and the meaning is: "possessing safety (salamah)",

﴿to a man﴾, that is: "having exclusive ownership of him, free from partnership". "Saliman" is read by Makki and Abu 'Amr, meaning: "purely his".

﴿Are the two equal in description?﴾, an adjective (sifah), and it is a specification (tamyiz). The meaning is: "Are their attributes and conditions equal?" He limited the specification to the singular only to indicate the category (li-bayan al-jins). It is also read "mathalayn" (two parables).

﴿Praise be to God﴾, who has no god but Him,

﴿but most of them do not know﴾, so they associate others with Him. He likened the disbeliever and his objects of worship (ma'budiyhi) to a slave in whom partners share, among whom there is dispute and disagreement, and each one of them claims that he is his slave. So they pull him in different directions and assign him to various tasks, while he is perplexed, not knowing which of them to please with his service, on which of them to rely for his needs, from whom to seek his provision, or from whom to seek his kindness. Thus his resolve is scattered, and his heart is divided. But the believer is like a slave who has one master, so his resolve is one and his heart is united.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 30:

﴿Indeed, you are dying﴾, i.e., you will die,

﴿and indeed they are dying﴾. With the light pronunciation (mayt), it means one upon whom death has descended. Al-Khalil said: Abu 'Amr recited:

Do you ask me to explain mayt and mayyit? Then take it from me; I have explained it, if you understand.
Whoever has a soul, that one is mayt (one who will die), ***
And the mayt is only one who is carried to the grave.

They were waiting for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to die, so he was informed that death will overtake them as well, so there is no sense in their waiting and gloating over one mortal by another mortal. And from Qatadah: "He informed His Prophet of his own self, and He informed you of your selves", i.e., you and they are counted among the dead, because what is certain to occur is as if it has already occurred.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 31:

﴿Then indeed you﴾ means: indeed you and they. The masculine second-person pronoun (addressing you) has been given precedence over the third-person pronoun (referring to them).

﴿On the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute﴾. You (the Prophet) will argue against them that you conveyed the message, but they denied it, and you exerted yourself in calling them, but they obstinately persisted in their stubbornness. They will offer excuses with what has no substance. The followers will say: "We obeyed our masters and our great ones," and the masters will say: "The devils misled us, and our forefathers of old." The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, said: "What dispute is there between us, when we are brothers?" Then when ʿUthman (may Allah be pleased with him) was killed, they said: "This is our dispute." It is also related from Abu al-ʿAliyah that the verse was revealed concerning the People of the Qiblah (the Muslims), and that it refers to the blood and the injustices that exist between them. The first interpretation is the more apparent, do you not see His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 32:

﴿So who is more unjust than one who lies against Allah﴾, and His saying: ﴿And he who brings the truth and confirms it﴾ [al-Zumar: 33]? This is only an explanation and clarification for those who are in dispute.

﴿Lies against Allah﴾: he fabricates against Him by ascribing to Him a son and a partner.

﴿And denies the truth﴾: the matter which is the truth itself, namely what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought.

﴿When it has come to him﴾: he confronted it with denial, upon hearing it, without pausing to employ deliberation or to take care to distinguish between truth and falsehood, as people of fairness do with what they hear. ﴿Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the disbelievers?﴾ That is: for these people who lied against Allah and denied the truth. The lam in "lil-kafirin" (for the disbelievers) is an indication referring to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 33:

﴿And he who brings the truth and confirms it﴾: he is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He brought the truth and believed in it, and by it he intended himself and whoever follows him, just as he intended Musa and his people by it in His saying: ﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book that they might be guided﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 49]. Therefore He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿Those are the God-fearing﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: It has been related from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "﴿He who brings the truth﴾ is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and ﴿he who confirms it﴾ is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him)." It has also been related that ﴿he who brings the truth﴾ is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and ﴿he who confirms it﴾ is the believers. All of these are sound, so they say. The preferred view in Arabic grammar (al-'arabiyya) is that "jaa'" (brought) and "saddaqa" (confirmed) have one subject, because difference would require an omitted "alladhi" (the relative pronoun), and that is not permissible, or an omitted subject without prior mention, and that is far-fetched.

The construction of "worst" (*aswa'*) and "best" (*ahsan*) with what follows them is an *idafah* (genitive construction) in which a thing is attributed to something that is part of it, without tafdil (comparative or superlative sense), as in your saying: "al-Ashajj is the most just of the Banu Marwan."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 36:

﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ The interrogative hamza of denial (hamzat al-inkar) has been placed before the negative word (kalimat al-nafy), so that it conveys the meaning of affirming sufficiency and establishing it.

﴿His servant﴾, i.e., Muhammad (ﷺ). Another reading is "ʿibādahu" (His servants), read by Hamza and ʿAlī, i.e., the prophets and the believers. It is like the verse: ﴿Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers﴾ [al-Hijr: 95]. (p-181) ﴿And they frighten you with those other than Him﴾, i.e., with the idols that they had taken as gods besides Him. That is because the Quraysh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We fear that our gods will afflict you with madness, and we fear for you their harm because of your reviling them."

﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾

And whoever Allah guides, none can lead astray. Is not Allah Almighty, Owner of Retribution?

﴿And whoever Allah guides, none can lead astray. Is not Allah Almighty﴾, meaning: "Mighty" (bi-ghalib mani'), one who overcomes and is invincible.

﴿Owner of Retribution﴾: He takes vengeance upon His enemies. In this there is a threat to Quraysh and a promise to the believers that He will avenge them upon them and give them victory over them. Then He informs that they, despite their worship of idols, acknowledge that Allah (Exalted) created the heavens and the earth, by His saying:

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 39, verse 38:**

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say: "Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah? If Allah intends harm for me,"﴾, with the yā' (ي) in *أرادنيَ* vowelled with a fatḥa (*بِفَتْحِ الياءِ*), except for Ḥamza (*سِوى حَمْزَةَ*),

﴿harm﴾, meaning sickness, poverty, or something else,

﴿"can they remove his harm?"﴾, meaning, can they repel its severity from me,

﴿"or if He intends mercy for me"﴾, meaning health, wealth, or the like,

﴿"can they withhold His mercy?"﴾ In *"kāshifātun ḍurrahu"* and *"mumsikātun raḥmatahu"* the words are read with tanwīn (nunation, *بِالتَنْوِينِ*), according to the original form (*عَلى الأصْلِ*). This is the reading of the Baṣrī (the school of Basra). He (the Prophet) was ordered to pose the question to himself, not to them, because they had frightened him with the harm of the idols and their power to afflict him (*لِأنَّهم خَوَّفُوهُ مَعَرَّةَ الأوْثانِ، وتَخْبِيلَها*). So he was commanded first to establish with them that the Creator of the world is Allah alone, and then, after this establishment, to say to them: "If the Creator of the world, whom you have acknowledged, intends harm or mercy for me, can they (your idols) prevent that?" When this silenced them, Allah (Exalted) said: ﴿Say: "Allah is sufficient for me"﴾, being sufficient to protect me from the harm of your idols,

﴿in Him the trusting put their trust﴾. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked them, they fell silent, and then ﴿Say: "Allah is sufficient for me"﴾ was revealed. He said *"kāshifāt"* and *"mumsikāt"* in the feminine form (*عَلى التَأْنِيثِ*) after His words ﴿And they frighten you with those besides Him﴾ [al-Zumar: 36], because they are females (*لِأنَّهُنَّ إناثٌ*), and they are: al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā, and Manāt. In this there is a mockery (*تَهَكُّمٌ*) of them and of what they worship.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 39:

(p-182) ﴿Say: "O my people, act according to your standing (makanah), indeed I am acting [according to mine]."﴾ That is: act upon your state in which you are, and your direction of enmity in which you have become firmly established. The word "makanah" (standing, position) carries the meaning of "makan" (place), so it is used figuratively for the sense [of place], just as "huna" (here) and "haythu" (where) are used for time, though both are [originally] for place.

﴿Indeed I am acting﴾, i.e., upon my standing. The object is omitted for brevity, and because of what it contains of increased threat, and of signalling that his state grows stronger every day, because Allah (Exalted) is his helper and supporter. Do you not see His saying: ﴿So you will come to know﴾?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 40:

﴿Whoever will be visited by a punishment that disgraces him, and upon him will descend a lasting punishment.﴾ How does He threaten them with His being victorious over them, dominant over them in this world and the Hereafter? Because when disgrace and punishment come upon them, that is His might and His triumph, inasmuch as victory is completed for Him through the might of a mighty one among His friends and the abasement of a debased one among His enemies. And "yukhzihi" (disgracing him) is an attribute of "adhab" (punishment), just like "muqim" (lasting), meaning: a punishment that disgraces him, and it is the Day of Badr; and a lasting punishment, which is the punishment of the Fire. "Makanatikum" (your positions), "Abu Bakr and Hammad" (the readings of Abu Bakr and Hammad).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 41:

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book﴾, i.e., the Qur'an,

﴿for mankind﴾, for their sake, and because of their need for it, so that they may be given glad tidings and be warned, whereby their inclinations towards choosing obedience over disobedience are strengthened,

﴿in truth. Whoever is guided, it is for his own self﴾, i.e., whoever chooses guidance has benefited his own self,

﴿And whoever goes astray, it is only to its own loss﴾, i.e., whoever chooses misguidance has harmed it,

﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾, i.e., a keeper (ḥafīẓ). Then he was informed that He is the Guardian (al-Ḥafīẓ), the Powerful over them, by His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 42:

﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾. "Al-anfus" (the souls): the persons themselves, as they are. "Tawaffi-ha" (taking them): causing them to die, which means removing that by which they are living, sensing and perceiving.

﴿And those that have not died in their sleep﴾. He takes the souls that have not died in their sleep, meaning He takes them when they sleep, likening sleepers to the dead, since they neither discern nor act, just as the dead do not. From this is His (Exalted) saying: ﴿It is He who takes you at night﴾ [al-An'am: 60]. ﴿Then He keeps﴾ the souls,

﴿those upon whom He has decreed death﴾. "Qudiya" (decreed) is read by Hamzah and Ali. The death is the real death, meaning He does not return it to life at its time.

﴿And He sends back the others﴾, the sleeping ones,

﴿until a specified term﴾, until a time He has set for their death. It is also said: "He takes the souls" means He completes them (yastawfi-ha), seizes them and takes them, and these are the souls in which life and movement remain. "And He takes the souls that have not died in their sleep" refers to the souls of discernment. They said: what is taken in sleep is the soul of discernment, not the soul of life, because when the soul of life departs, breath departs with it, and the sleeper breathes. Every person has two souls: one is the soul of life, which departs at death; the other is the soul of discernment, which departs from him when he sleeps. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "In the son of Adam there is a soul and a spirit, between which is a ray like the ray of the sun. The soul is that by which there is reason and discernment, and the spirit is that by which there is breath and motion. When the servant sleeps, Allah takes his soul and does not take his spirit." And from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The spirit leaves at sleep, and its ray remains in the body, and by that one sees dreams. When one is woken from sleep, the spirit returns to his body in less than the blink of an eye." And from him: "What the soul of the sleeper sees in the sky is the true dream, and what it sees after being sent back, Satan casts it, and it is false." And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that the spirits of the living and the spirits of the dead meet in sleep, and they become acquainted with whatever Allah wills them to become acquainted with, then He keeps the one upon which He has decreed death and sends back the others to their bodies until the end of the term of their lives. It is also narrated that the spirits of the believers ascend to the sky at sleep, and whoever among them is pure is permitted to prostrate, and whoever among them is not pure is not permitted to do so.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, indeed in the taking of souls, dead and sleeping, and their keeping and sending back until a term,

﴿are signs﴾, of the power and knowledge of Allah,

﴿for a people who reflect﴾, who turn their thoughts over in it and take lesson.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 43:

(p-184) ﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah?﴾ Rather, Quraysh took them. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for denial,

﴿besides Allah﴾, besides His permission,

﴿intercessors﴾, when they said: "These are our intercessors with Allah." Yet no one intercedes with Him except by His permission.

﴿Say: Even though they possess nothing and do not understand?﴾ Its meaning is: Will they intercede even though they possess nothing at all and have no understanding?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 44:

﴿Say, "To Allah belongs all intercession."﴾ That is: He is its Owner, so no one can intercede except by His permission. "Jami'an" (all together) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl),

﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth.﴾ This confirms His words ﴿To Allah belongs all intercession﴾, because if dominion entirely belongs to Him, and intercession is part of dominion, then He is its owner.

﴿Then to Him you will be returned.﴾ This is connected to what precedes it, meaning: to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth today, and then to Him you will be returned on the Day of Resurrection, so on that Day dominion belongs to none but Him. Thus to Him belongs the dominion of this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 45:

﴿And when Allah alone is mentioned⦈, the whole meaning turns on His words "alone" (waḥdah), i.e., when Allah is singled out for mention and their gods are not mentioned along with Him,

﴿are repulsed⦈, i.e., they recoil and are constricted,

﴿the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter. And when those other than Him are mentioned⦈, meaning their gods, if Allah is mentioned along with them or not mentioned,

﴿behold, they rejoice⦈, because of their infatuation with them. And when it is said, "There is no god but Allah, alone, without partner," they recoil, because it negates their gods. The opposites of rejoicing (istibshar) and repulsion (ishmi'zaz) are juxtaposed, since each of them is an extreme in its own domain. Istibshar is that the heart is filled with joy until the brightness of the face expands and glows, while ishmi'zaz is that one is filled with grief and rage until the contraction appears on the surface of the face. The governing element of "when it is mentioned" is the same as that governing "idha," the particle of suddenness (al-mufajaʾah), and its implied sense is: "At the time the ones other than Him are mentioned, they suddenly rejoice at the time of rejoicing."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 46:

﴿Say: O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth,﴾ meaning: "O Originator" (yā fāṭir). It is not an adjective, as al-Mubarrad and al-Farra' say.

﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed,﴾ the secret and the open.

﴿You judge,﴾ that is, You decide,

﴿between Your servants concerning that in which they differ.﴾ That is, concerning guidance and misguidance. It has also been said: this is a referral by the Prophet (ﷺ) of the polytheists to Allah.

It is narrated from al-Rabi' ibn al-Musayyib: "I do not know of any verse that is recited and then supplication is made at it except that it is answered, other than this one." And it is narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, who was a man of few words, that he was informed of the killing of al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with him), and they said: "Now he will speak." He said nothing more than: "Ah, have they really done it?!" Then he recited this verse. It is also narrated that he said after it: "Killed is the one whom he (ﷺ) used to seat on his lap and place his mouth upon his mouth."

The pronoun in "ومثله" refers back to "ما" (what is on the earth).

﴿Even if those who did wrong possessed everything on the earth, and the like of it along with it,﴾ ﴿they would surely ransom themselves with it from the evil of the punishment﴾ — that is, its severity — ﴿on the Day of Resurrection. And there will appear to them from Allah what they had not reckoned﴾ — and there will become apparent to them from the wrath of Allah and His punishment what had never been in their reckoning, nor did they even speak of it to themselves. It was also said: they did deeds that they considered good, but they turned out to be evil deeds.

It is narrated from Sufyan al-Thawri that he recited it and said: "Woe to the people of showing off (riya'), woe to the people of showing off." Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir became distressed at his death, and it was said to him (about this), so he said: "I fear a verse from the Book of Allah," and he recited it, "so I fear that there will appear to me from Allah what I had not reckoned."

And the evil deeds they had earned will become manifest to them, meaning: the evil consequences of their deeds that they had earned, or the evil of their earning, when the pages of their deeds are presented, and they had been hidden from them; or the punishment for that.

And what they used to mock at will encompass them, and descend upon them, and surround them,

the punishment for their mockery.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 49:

﴿When harm touches man, he calls on Us; then when We bestow on him a favour from Us﴾. That is: We give him, out of grace. It is said: "khawwalani" (he bestowed upon me), when someone gives you without any recompense,

﴿a favour from Us﴾. Do not pause on it, because the response of "idha" (when) is: ﴿he says, "I have only been given it on knowledge"﴾, meaning from Me, that I shall be given it because of the merit and entitlement that is in me, or "on knowledge" from me of the ways of earning, as Qarun said: ﴿on knowledge that is with me﴾ [al-Qasas: 78]. He used the pronoun in "utītuhu" (I have been given it), though its antecedent is "ni'mah" (favour), in view of the meaning, because (p-186) His saying "a favour from Us" means "some of the favour and a portion of it." It is also said that "ma" in "innama" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), not a restrictive particle (kaffah), so the pronoun refers back to it, meaning: "Indeed, that which I have been given, I have it on knowledge."

﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾: a rejection of his claim, as if He said: "We did not bestow on you the favour in the way you say; rather, it is a trial and a test for you: will you give thanks or will you disbelieve?" Since the predicate (khabar) is feminine, namely "fitnah" (trial), it is permissible to make the subject (mubtada') feminine on its account. It is also read: "Rather, it (huwa) is a trial," in agreement with "innama utitu-hu" (I have only been given it).

﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that it is a trial. The reason for connecting this verse with "fa" (then), and connecting its like at the beginning of the surah with "wa" (and), is that this verse came as a consequence (musabbabah) of His saying: ﴿And when God alone is mentioned, their hearts recoil﴾ [al-Zumar: 45], meaning that they recoil from the mention of God and rejoice at the mention of the gods. So when harm touches one of them, he calls upon the One whose mention made him recoil, not the one whose mention made him rejoice. What lies between them of verses is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD). If you say: the proper form of a parenthetical insertion is that it should emphasise what it interrupts, I say: in the parenthesis there is the Messenger's (ﷺ) supplication to his Lord, by a command from God, and his saying: "You judge between Your servants," and then the great threat that follows it, which is an emphasis on the denial of their recoiling, their rejoicing, and their turning to God in hardships rather than to their gods. It is as if it was said: "Say, O Lord, none judges between me and these people who dare against You with such audacity except You."

His saying: ﴿And if those who did wrong had all that is in the earth, and the like of it with it﴾ [al-Zumar: 47] applies to them, and to every wrongdoer if it is taken generally, or to them specifically if you intend them by it. It is as if it was said: "Even if these wrongdoers had all that is on earth together, and the like of it with it, they would ransom themselves with it when judgement is passed upon them of evil punishment."

As for the first verse, it was not a consequence; it is merely a sentence that corresponds to a sentence before it, so it is joined to it with "wa," like: "Zayd stood up and 'Amr sat down." The demonstration that it is a consequence is that you say: "Zayd believes in God, and when harm touches him he turns to Him," which is an evident causal link. Then you say: "Zayd disbelieves in God, and when harm touches him he turns to Him," and you bring in "fa" just as you brought it there, as if the disbeliever, when he turns to God with the turning of the believer, has placed his disbelief in the position of belief, by making it the cause of the turning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 50:

﴿Qad qālahā﴾: that is, this statement, namely his saying: "I have only been given it on account of knowledge" (innamā ūtītuhu ʿalā ʿilm),

﴿alladhīna min qablihim﴾: that is, Qarun and his people, when he said: ﴿"I have only been given it on account of knowledge I possess"﴾ [al-Qasas: 78]. His people were content with it, so it is as if they had said it themselves. It is also possible that among the earlier nations (al-umam al-khāliya) there were others who said the same thing,

﴿So what they used to earn did not avail them﴾, of the enjoyment of this world and what they gathered from it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 51:

﴿So the evil consequences of what they earned afflicted them.﴾ That is: the requital of the evil deeds of their earning. Or he called the requital of an evil deed an "evil deed" by way of mutual correspondence (izdiwaj, a stylistic pairing), as in His saying: ﴿And the requital of an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40]. ﴿And those who wronged﴾, [meaning] disbelieved,

﴿from among these﴾, that is: from among the polytheists of your people,

﴿the evil consequences of what they earned will afflict them﴾. That is: there will afflict them the like of what befell those [before them]. Their chieftains were slain at Badr, and provision was withheld from them so that they suffered drought for seven years.

﴿And they will not escape﴾, that is, they will not escape from the punishment of Allah. Then [provision] was expanded for them, and they were given rain for seven years. Then it was said to them:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 52:

﴿Do they not know that Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾, and restricts it. It was said: He makes it according to the measure of what is lost (al-fawt),

﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾, that there is no withholder and no extender except Allah, Exalted and Majestic.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 53:

﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, they have harmed themselves by excess in sins and by going to extremes in them,

﴿do not despair﴾, do not lose hope. (It is read with a kasra on the nun by ʿAlī and Baṣrī.)

﴿of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾, by pardoning them, except shirk. (It is read with the yāʾ sukūn by Baṣrī, Ḥamzah and ʿAlī.) In the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ): "He forgives sins, all of them, and does not mind." The counterpart of the negation of concern is the negation of fear in His saying: ﴿and He does not fear its consequence﴾ [al-Shams: 15]. It was said: it was revealed concerning Waḥshī, the slayer of Ḥamzah, may Allah be pleased with him. And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I would not love to have the world and everything in it in exchange for this verse."

﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving﴾, by covering up great sins,

﴿the Merciful﴾, by removing severe calamities.

﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, like His saying: ﴿Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾ [al-Zumar: 18]. And His saying ﴿before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾, i.e., it will overtake you while you are heedless, as if you fear nothing because of the extent of your negligence.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 39, verse 56:

﴿lest a soul should say﴾: lest it should say,

﴿a soul﴾: it is indefinite (*nakkirat*) because what is meant is some of the souls, namely the soul of the disbeliever. It is also permissible that what is meant is a soul distinguished from the rest of the souls, either by its extreme obstinacy in disbelief or by a great punishment. It is also permissible that what is meant is multiplicity.

﴿Alas, my regret!﴾: the *alif* (in *ya hasrata*) is a replacement for the *ya'* of the first person (the speaker's "my"). It is read as "*ya hasrati*", according to the original form, and as "*ya hasratayya*", combining the substitute (*'iwad*) with the thing it replaces (*mu'awwad minhu*).

﴿for what I neglected﴾: I fell short (*qassartu*). The *ma* is a verbal-nominal particle (*masdariyya*), like its use in ﴿with all its vastness﴾ [al-Tawba: 25].

﴿in the side of Allah﴾: in the matter of Allah, or in the obedience of Allah, or in His essence. In the reading of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is "in the remembrance of Allah". *Al-janb* means *al-janib* (the side, the direction). It is said: "I am in the side (*janb*) of so-and-so, and his flank (*janib*), and his region (*nahiya*)", and "so-and-so is gentle in his side and his flank." Then they said: "He neglected in his side and in his flank," meaning: in his right. This is from the figurative usage (*al-kinaya*, metonymy), because when you establish a matter in a man's place and his domain, you have established it in him. From this is the hadith: "Among hidden shirk is that a man prays for the sake of (*li-makan*) a man," meaning: for his sake. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: he neglected the path of Allah, which is His monotheism and the affirmation of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And indeed I was among the mockers﴾: among those who ridicule. Qatada said: "It was not enough for him that he neglected the obedience of Allah, until he mocked its people." The position (*mahall*) of ﴿and indeed I was﴾ is the accusative, as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), as if he had said: "I neglected while I was mocking," meaning: I neglected in the state of my mockery.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 57:

﴿Or that she should say: "Had Allah guided me,﴾ that is, given me guidance (hidaya),

﴿I would have been among the God-fearing (muttaqin)﴾, among those who guard themselves against shirk (associating partners with God). The Shaykh, the Imam Abu Mansur, may Allah have mercy on him (exalted is He), said: "This disbeliever has a better understanding of Allah's guidance than the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that held human beings must do what is good and right by their own capacity). Likewise are those disbelievers who said to their followers: ﴿Had Allah guided us, we would have guided you﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]. They are saying: Had Allah granted us success (tawfiq) in guidance and given us the right path, we would have called you to it. But He knew from us a choice of error and misguidance, so He forsook us and did not grant us success. The Mu'tazila say: Rather, He guided them and gave them success, but they did not become guided."

The conclusion is that with Allah there is a grace (lutf). Whoever is given it is guided, and that is tawfiq and protection (ismah). Whoever is not given it goes astray and errs, and his preference for punishment and his squandering of the truth occur after he had been enabled to attain it.

Or [lest] it say, when it sees the punishment: ﴿If only I had a return﴾, a return to the world,

﴿so that I might be among the doers of good﴾, among the monotheists.

"Bala" (بلى), a response from God, as if He were saying: ﴿Yes indeed, My verses came to you﴾ and I made clear to you the guidance from error, and the path of truth from falsehood, and I empowered you to choose guidance over error and truth over falsehood. But you neglected that and wasted it, you became arrogant in accepting it, you preferred misguidance over guidance, and you occupied yourself with the opposite of what you were commanded. So the waste came from your side, and you have no excuse. And "bala" is an answer to an implied negation, because the meaning is: "If God had guided me," (you would say) "I would not have been guided." He did not attach the answer to it because the sayings of the soul must be related in their order, and then the answer comes from among them, concerning what the answer required.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 60:

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied about Allah﴾, ascribing to Him what is not befitting for Him, such as associating partners with Him and attributing children to Him, and denying His attributes.

﴿Their faces﴾ is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence),

﴿blackened﴾ is the khabar (predicate), and the sentence is in the place of a nasb (accusative) as a hal (circumstantial clause), if "tara" (you see) is from the sight of the eye (ru'yat al-basar, visual seeing). If it is from the sight of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb, mental seeing), then it is the second maf'ul (object).

﴿Is there not in Hell an abode﴾ is a munzal (a state of lodging or stopping), 

﴿for the arrogant?﴾ It refers to His saying: "and you were arrogant."

And Allah will save (﴿وَيُنَجِّي اللهُ﴾), that is, He will save the spirit (rūḥ) of

﴿those who were mindful of Allah﴾ (﴿الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا﴾), from polytheism (shirk),

﴿with their salvation﴾ (﴿بِمَفازَتِهِمْ﴾), that is, with their success (falāḥ). It is said "fāza bi-kadhā" (he succeeded in such-and-such) when he achieved success through it and attained his aim from it. The explanation of mafāza is: ﴿evil will not touch them﴾ (﴿لا يَمَسُّهُمُ السُوءُ﴾), namely, the Fire,

﴿nor will they grieve﴾ (﴿وَلا هم يَحْزَنُونَ﴾). It is as if it were said: "What is their mafāza?" and the answer was: "Evil will not touch them." That is, He saves them by negating evil and grief from them, meaning no harm touches their bodies and no disgrace touches their hearts. Or it means "because of their deliverance," from His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Do not think them secure from the punishment﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 188), that is, secure from it, because deliverance is among the greatest success. The cause of their deliverance is righteous deeds. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, explained mafāza as good deeds. It is also permissible that it means "because of their success," since righteous deeds are the cause of success, which is entering Paradise. It is also permissible that righteous deeds themselves be called "mafāza," because they are its cause.

The phrase "lā yamassuhum" has no grammatical position (maḥall) according to the first explanation, because it is a resumptive (mustaʾnaf) sentence. According to the second explanation its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), reading "bi-mafāzātihim" (with their salvations) in the plural. This is the reading of the Kufan reader other than Ḥafs (kūfiyyun ghayra Ḥafṣ).

﴿Allah is the Creator of all things﴾: a refutation of the Mu'tazilah and the Thanawiyya (Dualists).

﴿And He is, over all things, a Wakil﴾: a Guardian (ḥāfiẓ).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 63:

﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is: He is the owner of their affairs and their guardian. This is a case of *kinaya* (metonymy, an indirect expression), because the keeper of treasuries and the one who manages their affairs is the one who holds their keys (*maqalid*). From this is the saying of people: "So-and-so has been handed the keys (*maqalid*) of rule." The singular of *maqalid* is *miqlid*, meaning key. It was also said that the word has no singular from its own root, and that the word is originally Persian.

﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah, they are the losers.﴾ This is connected to His words: "And Allah will deliver those who were mindful of Him." That is: Allah will deliver the God-fearing (*muttaqin*) by their achievements (*mafazat*), and those who disbelieved are the losers. Between the two, an objection is raised: that He is the Creator of everything, and so He has dominion over it, and nothing of the deeds of the responsible persons (*mukallafin*) is hidden from Him, nor what they will be recompensed for. Or [the connection is] with what follows it: that everything in the heavens and the earth has Allah as its Creator and the One who opens its door.

﴿And those who disbelieved﴾ and denied that the matter is so,

﴿they are the losers.﴾ It was also said: "Uthman asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the interpretation of His words: ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾, and he said: 'O Uthman, no one has asked me about this before you. Its interpretation is: There is no god but Allah, Allah is the Greatest, Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him, I seek the forgiveness of Allah, and there is no power and no strength except through Allah. He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward. In His hand is good. He gives life and causes death, and He is powerful over everything.'" Its interpretation according to this is that these words belong to Allah, by which He is declared one and glorified, and they are the keys to the good of the heavens and the earth. Whoever among the God-fearing speaks them will attain [that good].

﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah﴾ and the words of His oneness and glorification,

﴿they are the losers.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 64:

﴿Say﴾, to those who invite you to the religion of your fathers:

﴿Do you order me to worship other than Allah?﴾ "تَأْمُرُونِّي" (ta'murūnnī) is read by Makki with the doubled nun; "تَأْمُرُونَنِي" (ta'murūnanī) is read on the original form; Shami reads "تَأْمُرُونِيَ" (ta'murūnī); Madani reads "تَأْمُرُونِيَ" (ta'murūnī). "أفَغَيْرَ اللهِ" is governed in the accusative by "أعْبُدُ" (a'budu, "I worship"), and "تَأْمُرُونِّي" is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraḍ, a phrase inserted between parts of a sentence). Its meaning is: "Do I worship other than Allah at your command after this clarification?!"

﴿O you ignorant ones﴾, regarding the oneness of Allah.

﴿And it has certainly been revealed to you and to those before you﴾, [that is, to] the prophets, peace be upon them,

﴿"If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be nullified, and you will certainly be among the losers"﴾. He said "if you associate partners" in the singular, [referring to] tawhid (affirming the oneness of God), while those to whom it was revealed are a group, because its meaning is: "It has been revealed to you, [saying] 'If you associate partners, your deeds will surely be nullified,' and to those before you the same." The first لام (lam) is the lam of preparation (موطِّئة) for the implied oath (qasam), and the second is the lam of the response (لام الجواب). This response takes the place of both responses, namely the response of the oath and the response of the condition (sharṭ). This statement is valid even though God knows that His messengers do not associate partners, because the address (الخطاب) is to the Prophet ﷺ while the intended meaning is someone else, and because it is in the form of a supposition (فرض), and impossible things may be supposed. It was also said: "If you examine someone other than Me in secret, the secret matters between Me and you will be nullified."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 66:

﴿Rather, worship Allah﴾, is a rejection of what they urged him to do, namely worship of their gods. It is as if He said: "Do not worship what they urge you to worship; rather, if you are going to worship, then worship Allah." So He omitted the condition, and placed the fronting of the object (al-mafʿul, the object of the verb) in its place as a substitute for it,

﴿and be among the grateful﴾, for what He has bestowed upon you, namely that He made you the master of the children of Adam.

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾, and they did not magnify Him with His true magnificence, when they called you to worship other than Him. Since the great thing among things, when a person knows it with true knowledge and esteems it in his soul with true esteem, magnifies it with true magnification, it was said: "They did not measure God with His true measure." Then He alerted them to His greatness and the sublimity of His station, by way of takhyil (imaginative representation), so He said: ﴿The whole earth will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾. The purpose of this statement, if you take it as it is in its entirety and as a whole, is to depict His greatness and to make people aware of the reality of His majesty, and nothing else, without taking the handful or the right hand toward a literal direction or a figurative direction. By "the earth" is meant the seven earths. This is supported by His saying "all together" and by His saying "and the heavens," and because the context is one of magnification, which calls for emphasis (al-mubalaghah). "Al-ard" (the earth) is the subject (mubtada'), "qabdatuhu" (His handful) is the predicate (khabar), and "jami'an" (all together) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), meaning: "The earth, when it is gathered together, is His handful on the Day of Resurrection." "Al-qabdah" is the single instance of "al-qabd" (grasping), and "al-qubdah" is the amount grasped in the palm. One says, "Give me a qabdah of such-and-such," meaning "al-qubdah," naming it by the verbal noun. Both meanings are possible. The meaning is: "The earths, all together, are His handful," that is, "possessors of His handful," He grasps them in one handful. The meaning is that the earths, despite their greatness and expanse, do not amount to more than one handful of His handfuls, as if He grasps them in one palm, just as one says, "The slaughtered camel is the meal of Luqman," meaning it suffices for only one single morsel of his meals. And if the meaning of "al-qubdah" is intended, it is clear, because the meaning is that the earths in their totality are the quantity He grasps with one palm. "Al-matwiyyat" (the folded ones) derives from "al-tayy" (folding), which is the opposite of "al-nashr" (spreading), as He said: (p-193) ﴿On the day We roll up the heaven like the rolling up of a written scroll﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104]. The customary way of one who folds a scroll is to fold it with his right hand. It is also said: "qabdatuhu" means "His possession," without any repeller or contender. And "bi-yaminihi" means "by His power." It is also said: "matwiyyat bi-yaminihi" means "annihilated by His oath," because He swore that He would annihilate them.

﴿Glory be to Him, and high is He above what they associate with Him﴾. How far is He from one whose power and greatness are such! And how exalted is He above the partners that are ascribed to Him!

The Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 68:

﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, so whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom Allah wills﴾, that is, died.

﴿Except whom Allah wills﴾, that is: Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and the Angel of Death. It is said: they are the bearers of the Throne, or Ridwan, and the maidens of paradise (al-Hur al-'In), and Malik, and the Zabaniyah.

﴿Then it will be blown again, another time﴾. The word "another" (ukhra) is in the place of nominative case (mahall al-raf'), because the meaning is: "And the Trumpet will be blown with one blast, then it will be blown again with another blast." The second blast's verb was omitted because of the indication of "another" (ukhra) upon it, and because it is known from its mention in more than one place.

﴿Then, behold, they will be standing, looking on﴾, they will be turning their eyes in all directions, like the gaze of one bewildered when a calamity suddenly strikes him; or, they will be looking at the command of Allah concerning them. The verse indicates that the blasts are two: the first for death, and the second for resurrection. The majority of scholars hold that they are three: the first for terror (al-faza'), as He said: ﴿And the day the Trumpet is blown, so terrified will be whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾ [al-Naml: 87]; the second for death; and the third for re-creation (al-i'adah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 69:

﴿And the earth shall shine with the light of its Lord﴾, i.e., it shall be illuminated (أضاءَتْ),

﴿with the light of its Lord﴾, i.e., with His justice (بِعَدْلِهِ), by way of metaphor (بِطَرِيقِ الِاسْتِعارَةِ). It is said to the just ruler: "The horizons have shone with your justice, and the world has been illuminated with your equity," just as it is said: "The lands have been darkened by the oppression of so-and-so." He - upon him be blessings and peace - said: « "Injustice is darkness on the Day of Resurrection." » The attribution of His name to the earth is because He adorns it, in that He spreads His justice in it, sets up the scales of His equity in it, and judges with truth among its people. You will not see anything more adorning to places than justice, nor anything that makes them more prosperous than it. The Imam Abu Mansur - may Allah have mercy on him - said: "It is permissible that Allah creates a light and illuminates with it the place of standing (أرْضَ المَوْقِفِ)." Its attribution to Him (exalted is He) is for specification (لِلتَّخْصِيصِ), like "the House of Allah" (بَيْتُ اللهِ) and "the she-camel of Allah" (ناقَةُ اللهِ),

(p-194)

﴿And the Book will be placed﴾, i.e., the pages of deeds (صَحائِفُ الأعْمالِ), but He suffices with the generic noun (اسْمِ الجِنْسِ), or it is the Preserved Tablet (اللَوْحُ المَحْفُوظُ),

﴿and the prophets will be brought﴾, so that their Lord may ask them about the conveyance of the message and what their peoples answered them,

﴿and the witnesses﴾, the guardian angels (الحَفَظَةِ). It is said: they are the righteous of every age, who bear witness over the people of that age,

﴿and it will be judged between them﴾, between the servants,

﴿with truth﴾, with justice,

﴿and they will not be wronged﴾. He concluded the verse with the negation of injustice, just as He opened it with the affirmation of justice.

﴿And every soul will be paid in full for what it did﴾, that is, its recompense,

﴿and He is most knowing of what they do﴾, without a record, and without a witness. It was also said: this verse is an explanation of His words, "and they will not be wronged", meaning: "every soul will be paid in full for what it did, of good and evil, without any increase in evil and without any decrease in good."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 71:

﴿And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell﴾, driven harshly, as prisoners are driven, and those who rebel against the ruler, when they are led to prison or to execution,

﴿in groups﴾, a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: in companies, dispersed, one following another,

﴿until, when they reach it, its gates are opened﴾, read with light vowelling (takhfīf) in both places, according to al-Kūfī (the reading of the Kufan transmitters),

﴿its gates﴾, and they are seven,

﴿and its keepers will say to them﴾, that is, the guardians of Hell, who are the angels appointed to punish its inhabitants,

﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you﴾, from the children of Adam,

﴿reciting to you the signs of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this your day﴾, that is, this your time, which is the time of their entry into the Fire, not the Day of Resurrection,

﴿They will say: Yes﴾, they came to us and recited to us,

﴿But the word of punishment has become due against the disbelievers﴾, that is, but the word of Allah has become binding upon us: ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ [Hud: 119], because of the evil of our deeds, as they said: ﴿Our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a people astray﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 106]. Thus they mentioned their deed which necessitated the word of punishment, which is disbelief and misguidance.

﴿It shall be said: Enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein.﴾ "Khalidina fiha" is a circumstantial clause (hal) that is predicated (muqaddara), meaning "intending to abide" (muqaddirina al-khulud).

﴿So evil is the abode of the arrogant.﴾ The alif-lam in "al-mutakabbirin" is for the category (li-l-jins), because "mathwa al-mutakabbirin" is the agent (fa'il) of "bi'sa." "Bi'sa" has as its agent a noun defined by the alif-lam of category, or one that is annexed to a similar noun. The thing being censured (al-makhsus bi-l-dhamm) is omitted, and its estimated form is: "So evil is the abode of the arrogant, Hell."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 73:

﴿And those who had feared their Lord will be driven to the Garden in groups﴾. "Driven" means that their mounts are driven, because they are not taken there except as riders, to the abode of honour and good pleasure, as is done with one who is honoured and distinguished among the delegates who come to some of the kings.

﴿Until, when they reach it﴾. This is the particle (hatta, "until") after which sentences are related, and the sentences related after it are conditional sentences, except that its response (jaza', the apodosis) is omitted. It was omitted because it concerns the reward of the people of the Garden, so by omitting it, it indicates that it is something that description cannot encompass. Al-Zajjaj said: its estimated form is: "Until, when they reach it, and its gates are opened, and its guardians say to them, 'Peace be upon you; you are good, so enter it, abiding forever,' they entered it." So he omitted "they entered it," because there is an indication of it in the speech. Others said: "Until, when they reach it, they reach it, and its gates are opened." So for them "they reach it" is omitted, and the meaning is: "until, when they reach it, their arrival coincides with the opening of its gates." It was also said: the gates of Hell are not opened except when its people enter it, but the opening of the gates of the Garden precedes their arrival, due to His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Gardens of Eden, whose doors are opened for them﴾ [Sad: 50]. Therefore the waw (and) was used, as if He said: "Until, when they reach it, and its gates have already been opened."

﴿You are good﴾, from the defilement of sins, and you have been purified from the impurity of errors. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, you were good in the world, and you were not evil, that is, you were not people of wickedness. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The stay has become good for you." He made the entry into the Garden a consequence of goodness and purity, because it is the abode of the good and the dwelling place of the pure. Allah has purified it from every defilement and made it good from every filth, so none enters it except one who is suited to it and described by its qualities.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 39, verse 74:

﴿And they will say: "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us"﴾: He fulfilled for us what He promised us in this world, of the bliss of the final abode (al-'Uqba).

﴿And has made us inherit the land﴾: the land of Paradise. They have been made to inherit it, meaning they have come to possess it. They have been made its kings, and their disposal of it has been left unrestricted, so they do as they wish. This is a likeness to the state of the heir and his disposal of what he inherits and his freedom in it.

﴿We dwell (natabawwa')﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿in the Garden wherever we will﴾: (p-196) meaning that each one of them will have a garden of such vast extent that it cannot be described, and beyond what is needed. So he takes up dwelling (yatabawwa', i.e., yattakhidh, takes for himself) a place of residence and a station in his garden wherever he wills.

﴿How excellent is the reward of those who work﴾: in this world, namely the Garden.

﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne﴾: ﴿حافِّينَ﴾ (ḥāffīn, surrounding) is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause, glossed as the grammatical state of the subject) from ﴿المَلائِكَةَ﴾ (the angels).

﴿مِن حَوْلِ العَرْشِ﴾ means: encircling it on all sides. The ﴿مِن﴾ (min) indicates *ibtidāʾ al-ghāya* (the starting point of a limit), meaning that their encircling begins from around the Throne and extends to wherever Allah wills.

﴿يُسَبِّحُونَ﴾ (yusabbiḥūna, they glorify) is a *ḥāl* from the pronoun in ﴿حافِّينَ﴾ (ḥāffīn).

﴿بِحَمْدِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ (with the praise of their Lord) means: they say, "Glory be to Allah, and all praise is for Allah, and there is no god but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest," or they say, "Most Holy, Most Pure, Lord of the angels and the Spirit." This is for enjoyment, not as worship, because the obligation (*taklīf*) has ceased.

﴿وَقُضِيَ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ (and judgment will be passed between them) refers to judgment between the prophets and the nations, or between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire.

﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾ (with truth) means: with justice.

﴿وَقِيلَ الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ (and it will be said, "All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds") means: the people of Paradise will say it in gratitude upon entering it, and the promise of Allah to them will have been fulfilled. This is like His saying: ﴿وَآخِرُ دَعْواهم أنِ الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ (And the last of their prayer will be: "All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds") [Yunus: 10].

"The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite each night *Banī Isrāʾīl* and *al-Zumar*."
